title: Design an Ad Click Aggregator
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: redirect clicks fast, stream them through Kafka, count once per click ID in event-time windows, tame hot ads and reconcile billed numbers in batch.
body:
## Practice first

Design a system that records every click on an ad, sends the user on to the advertiser's landing page, and lets advertisers query click counts for their ads over time (for example, clicks per minute for the last hour, or per day for the last quarter). Advertisers are billed from these numbers, so accuracy matters.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching first: the click path, where events go after the click, how counts are produced, and how an advertiser query is answered quickly. Then read on. Most of the difficulty is in correctness of a streaming count (duplicates, late events, crashes), not in storing rows.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Click an ad and be redirected** to the advertiser's landing page.
2. **Have the click recorded** exactly once in the aggregate counts, even if they double-click or the system retries.
3. **Query aggregated metrics** (as an advertiser): clicks per ad or campaign over a time range at minute, hour or day granularity, optionally filtered by a small set of dimensions such as country or device.

Out of scope: impression tracking, conversion attribution, the billing system itself, machine-learning fraud detection (we leave a hook for it), and ad serving/auctions.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 10,000 clicks/s on average, 50,000/s at peak; about 10 million active ads.
- **Redirect latency:** p99 under 100 ms for the click redirect; recording the click must not add noticeably to it.
- **Freshness:** aggregates queryable within about 1 minute of the click (the dashboard is near-real-time).
- **Accuracy and durability, per operation:** the click path favours availability (never break the redirect) but must durably capture every click it acknowledges. Aggregates must be exactly-once *in effect*: no lost clicks, no double counting. Short-term numbers may be slightly incomplete; the final billed numbers must be correct.
- **Query latency:** p99 under 1 s for dashboard queries over up to 90 days.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Event volume:** 10,000/s × 86,400 s ≈ **864 million clicks/day**. At about 200 bytes per event, that is roughly **170 GB/day** raw, about 60 TB/year. Raw events go to cheap object storage; we never query them on the dashboard path.
- **Ingest bandwidth at peak:** 50,000 × 200 B = **10 MB/s**. A modest Kafka cluster handles this easily; partition count is chosen for consumer parallelism (say 64 partitions), not raw throughput.
- **Aggregate size:** minute buckets for 10 million ads would be 14.4 billion rows/day if every ad were clicked every minute, but clicks are sparse: realistically a few hundred thousand ads are clicked in any minute, so perhaps 200 to 400 million minute rows/day. That is why we roll up minutes into hours and days and expire minute data after a few weeks.
- **Skew:** a viral ad may get 5,000 clicks/s, half the average total, on one key. That forces the hot-key deep dive.

## Core entities

- **Ad:** ad ID, campaign ID, advertiser ID, landing URL.
- **Click event:** click ID (unique), ad ID, impression ID, user or device token, event timestamp, ingest timestamp, country, device.
- **Aggregate:** ad ID, time bucket (minute, hour or day), dimension values, click count, and version or source (streaming vs reconciled).

## API

```http
GET /c/{clickToken}
-> 302 Location: https://advertiser.example/landing?...
   (clickToken is a signed, short-lived token minted at impression time:
    adId, impressionId, clickId, expiry, HMAC)

GET /v1/ads/{adId}/metrics?from=2026-10-01T00:00Z&to=2026-10-29T00:00Z&granularity=hour&groupBy=country
Authorization: Bearer <advertiser token>
-> 200 { "adId": "ad_9", "granularity": "hour",
         "series": [{ "bucket": "2026-10-01T00:00Z", "country": "US", "clicks": 1832 }],
         "complete": false, "nextCursor": null }
```

The click endpoint is a browser redirect, so it is a `GET` that returns `302`, never `301` (browsers cache 301s, so repeat clicks would never reach us). The metrics endpoint is authorised per advertiser and returns a `complete` flag indicating whether the range includes buckets not yet reconciled.

## High-level design

**Click and redirect.** The ad's link points at our **click service**, not straight at the advertiser. The click service verifies the token's signature and expiry, looks up the landing URL (cached), publishes a click event, and returns a 302. Pointing at our service (server-side redirect) rather than having the browser send a beacon is what makes the count trustworthy: ad blockers and closed tabs drop client-side beacons.

**Record the click.** Instead of writing each click to a database (50,000 writes/s of tiny rows, contended per ad), the click service appends an event to a **Kafka** topic partitioned by ad ID. Kafka is the durable buffer: once the produce is acknowledged (with `acks=all`), the click is safe.

**Aggregate and query.** A **stream processor** consumes the topic, de-duplicates by click ID, and counts clicks per ad per one-minute window, writing results to an **OLAP store** (ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot) optimised for time-range aggregations. A connector also archives raw events to **object storage**, which a **batch job** uses to recompute and reconcile counts. The **query service** reads only the OLAP store.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["User browser"] -->|"GET /c/token"| CS["Click service"]
    CS -->|"302 redirect"| U
    CS --> K[["Kafka: clicks (by adId)"]]
    K --> SP["Stream processor (dedupe, 1-min windows)"]
    SP --> O[("OLAP store")]
    K --> Arch["Archiver"]
    Arch --> S3[("Object storage: raw events")]
    S3 --> BJ["Reconciliation batch job"]
    BJ --> O
    A["Advertiser dashboard"] --> QS["Query service"]
    QS --> O
```

Walk a click through it: the user clicks, the browser hits `/c/{token}`, the click service validates the HMAC, emits `{clickId, adId, ts, ...}` to Kafka and redirects in about 20 ms. Within a minute the stream processor closes that minute's window for the ad and upserts the count into the OLAP store. The advertiser's query reads minute rows for recent ranges and hourly/daily rollups for older ranges.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant C as Click service
    participant K as Kafka
    participant L as Landing page
    B->>C: GET /c/token
    C->>C: verify HMAC and expiry
    C->>K: produce click event (acks=all)
    K-->>C: ack
    C-->>B: 302 Location landing URL
    B->>L: GET landing page
```

If Kafka is briefly unavailable, the click service should still redirect (availability of the user path wins) and buffer the event to local disk for later replay, with an alert. Losing the redirect costs the advertiser a customer; delaying a count costs nothing.

## Deep dives

### 1. Exactly-once counting: dedupe and idempotent sinks

**Problem.** Duplicates enter at three places: users double-click (same impression clicked twice), clients or proxies retry the click request, and the stream processor itself replays events after a crash. Billing requires each logical click to count once.

**Bad: count every event, trust the pipeline.** Double-clicks and replays inflate counts, and advertisers dispute bills.

**Good: dedupe by click ID in the stream processor.** The click ID is minted at impression time and embedded in the signed token, so every request for the same impression carries the same ID. The processor keeps keyed state of recently seen click IDs (for example, for 1 hour, enough to cover double-clicks and retries), and drops repeats. A Bloom filter per time bucket can shrink this state at the cost of a tiny false-drop rate; an exact set is affordable here (about 36 million IDs per hour at 10,000/s).

**Great: dedupe plus checkpointed state plus an idempotent sink.** Dedupe only works if a crash does not reset it. Stream frameworks such as Flink snapshot operator state together with Kafka consumer offsets; on failure they restore both and replay from the saved offsets, so state and input stay consistent. The remaining gap is the sink: replayed windows are written again. Make the write an **upsert keyed by (adId, bucket, dimensions)** that sets the count rather than incrementing it, or use transactional sinks committed with the checkpoint. Then replays are harmless.

Also note the signed token: requiring a valid HMAC and short expiry blocks forged clicks with arbitrary IDs. Per-IP and per-device rate checks feed a fraud flag rather than silently dropping clicks, so finance can audit the decision.

### 2. Windows, event time and late events

**Problem.** A click at 12:00:58 may arrive at 12:01:20 because of mobile network delay or a Kafka consumer lag spike. Bucketing by arrival time (processing time) puts it in the wrong minute; waiting forever for stragglers means windows never close.

**Approach.** Bucket by **event time** (the click timestamp captured by the click service, not the browser's clock, which can be wrong). Use **tumbling one-minute windows** keyed by ad ID. The processor tracks a **watermark**, an estimate that "all events up to time T have probably arrived", typically the maximum event time seen minus a bound such as 30 s. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window fires and its count is written.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E["Click events (event time)"] --> WM["Watermark = max event time minus 30s"]
    WM --> Win["1-min tumbling window per adId"]
    Win -->|"watermark passes window end"| Emit["Emit count, upsert OLAP"]
    E --> Late{"Event older than window end plus allowed lateness?"}
    Late -->|"no"| Upd["Re-fire window with updated count"]
    Late -->|"yes"| Side[["Late-events side output"]]
    Side --> Recon["Corrected by reconciliation job"]
```

Events within the watermark bound land in their window normally. Events after the window fired but within an **allowed lateness** (say 5 minutes) cause the window to re-fire with an updated count, which the idempotent upsert absorbs. Anything later goes to a side output and is fixed by the batch reconciliation. The trade-off is explicit: a bigger watermark delay means fewer corrections but staler dashboards.

### 3. Hot ads: spreading a single key

**Problem.** Partitioning by ad ID keeps an ad's counts on one processor, which is simple and makes dedupe local. A viral ad at 5,000 clicks/s pins one partition and one task while the rest idle, and lag grows only for that ad.

**Bad: bigger machines.** Vertical scaling buys a little time; it does not fix skew.

**Good: salt hot keys.** Detect hot ads (a heavy-hitter counter on the click service or a configured list) and key them as `adId:n` with n in 0..N-1, spreading clicks over N partitions. Each sub-key is counted independently, and a second, small aggregation step sums the N partial counts per window before writing. Dedupe still works if the salt is derived from the click ID (`hash(clickId) mod N`), so duplicates of the same click land on the same sub-key.

**Great: salting plus local pre-aggregation.** Each processor task first combines counts in memory for a few seconds (a "combiner"), so the shuffle carries one partial count per key per task instead of one message per click. With both, hot keys cost about the same as normal ones.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    K[["Clicks for hot ad 9"]] --> S0["Sub-key 9:0 count"]
    K --> S1["Sub-key 9:1 count"]
    K --> S2["Sub-key 9:2 count"]
    K --> S3["Sub-key 9:3 count"]
    S0 --> M["Merge per window: sum partials"]
    S1 --> M
    S2 --> M
    S3 --> M
    M --> O[("OLAP: ad 9, minute bucket")]
```

The salt is chosen by click ID so each logical click always maps to the same sub-key; the merge step is cheap because it sees only N numbers per window.

### 4. Reconciliation: streaming is fast, batch is authoritative

**Problem.** Even with checkpoints and dedupe, streaming results can drift: very late events, a bad deploy that dropped a dimension, a bug in dedupe. Billing needs a number you can defend.

**Lambda architecture:** run the streaming path for freshness and a periodic batch job (for example, hourly and nightly with Spark) that recomputes counts from the raw events in object storage. Batch results overwrite the streaming rows for closed periods and mark them `reconciled`. A comparison report flags buckets where the two differ by more than a threshold, which doubles as a pipeline health check. The cost is two code paths that must implement identical logic.

**Kappa architecture:** keep one streaming code path and, when you need to correct history, replay the retained Kafka log (or the archived events) through a new version of the job into a fresh table, then swap. Simpler logic, but it requires long log retention or replay from storage and enough capacity to reprocess quickly.

**Recommendation for this prompt:** a streaming path for the dashboard plus a batch reconciliation for billing. Money justifies the duplicated logic; share the dedupe and bucketing code as a library to keep the paths aligned. The API's `complete` flag tells advertisers which numbers are final.

### 5. Fast queries over 90 days

**Problem.** A dashboard asking for 90 days of hourly clicks by country should not scan billions of minute rows.

Store aggregates in a columnar **OLAP store** partitioned by day and sorted by (advertiser, ad, bucket). Maintain **rollups**: minute rows for the last 14 days, hourly rows for 2 years, daily rows indefinitely. The query service picks the coarsest table that satisfies the requested granularity, so a 90-day hourly query touches about 2,160 rows per ad and dimension. Cache common dashboard queries for 30 to 60 seconds. Limit `groupBy` to low-cardinality dimensions decided up front; arbitrary slicing over raw events is an offline analytics product, not this API.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a server-side redirect, an event stream rather than per-click database writes, a stream job that counts by minute, and an OLAP store for queries.
- **Senior:** drives exactly-once semantics end to end (click ID minted at impression, deduped state, checkpoints, idempotent upserts), explains event time, watermarks and late data, and handles hot ads with salting and pre-aggregation.
- **Staff:** frames streaming vs batch as a freshness vs auditability decision tied to billing, designs reconciliation and its alerting, considers fraud hooks, retention costs and how to replay history safely after a bug.

## Common mistakes

- Incrementing a counter row in a relational database on every click.
- Using `301` for the click redirect, or a client-side beacon, and losing clicks.
- Saying "Kafka is exactly-once" and stopping there; duplicates from double-clicks and sink replays remain.
- Bucketing by processing time, so lag spikes shift clicks between minutes.
- Ignoring hot keys when partitioning by ad ID.
- Having no reconciliation story for the numbers advertisers are billed on.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] The redirect never depends on the counting pipeline being healthy.
- [ ] Every click carries a unique, signed ID created before the click happens.
- [ ] Dedupe state and consumer offsets are checkpointed together, and sink writes are idempotent.
- [ ] Windows use event time, with a stated watermark delay and late-event policy.
- [ ] Hot ads are spread with salted keys and merged per window.
- [ ] Batch reconciliation produces the billed numbers, and the API exposes completeness.
- [ ] Query paths use rollups sized to the requested range.

## Further reading

- [Apache Flink documentation: timely stream processing](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/time/)
- [Apache Kafka documentation](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
- [ClickHouse documentation](https://clickhouse.com/docs)
keyTakeaways: Record clicks with a server-side 302 redirect and an append to a durable log, never a per-click counter update in a database.
Exactly-once in effect needs a click ID minted before the click, deduplicated state checkpointed with offsets, and idempotent upserts at the sink.
Bucket by event time with watermarks; state the watermark delay, the allowed lateness and where very late events go.
Salt hot ad keys by click ID and merge partial counts per window so one viral ad cannot pin a partition.
Use streaming for freshness and batch reconciliation from raw events for the numbers you bill on.
